narrative:
The model determined that you have an 84% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class standing in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. These two academic performance measures outweighed everything else. Your LSAT score was the third most influential factor, but it worked in the opposite direction, giving a modest boost toward passing.

In practical terms, your placement in the second decile for both first- and third-year grades is well below the average performance of students who were accepted. While your LSAT score of 40 is actually higher than the average of accepted students (37.18), it was not enough to overcome the effect of your lower class rankings.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA, and plan to attend full-time had very little impact on the final decision.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the bar exam preparation courses or seeking additional support before reapplying. Improving your class standing in future semesters could significantly change how a similar model evaluates your application. (218 words)
